_fileVersion.notes: Attack Flows v1 – seven common attack patterns with multi-perspective phases

attacks.name: Phishing
attacks.short_description: Social engineering attack that tricks victims into revealing credentials or installing malware through deceptive emails, messages, or websites.

attacker.title: Gathering Intelligence on the Target
attacker.description: The attacker begins by collecting publicly available information about the target organization and its employees. This process, known as OSINT (Open Source Intelligence), involves scraping LinkedIn profiles, corporate websites, social media accounts, and even data breach dumps to learn names, job titles, email formats, and internal tools. The goal is to build a detailed profile so the eventual phishing message feels authentic and personally relevant. The more an attacker knows about a target, the more convincing the lure becomes.
tools_or_indicators: theHarvester, an email and subdomain enumeration tool that queries search engines and public data sources
Maltego, a visual link-analysis tool that maps relationships between people, domains, and organizations
LinkedIn and social media scraping
Hunter.io for discovering corporate email formats
Recon-ng, a modular reconnaissance framework

defender.title: Reducing Your Public Footprint and Detecting Profiling
defender.description: The most effective thing you can do during the reconnaissance phase is make the attacker's job harder before they even start. Conduct your own OSINT against your organization — run theHarvester or Hunter.io against your own domain and see what comes back. Anything an attacker can find, you can remove or obscure first. WAF logs will show automated scraping patterns: many requests in rapid succession, unusual User-Agent strings, or systematic traversal of employee directory pages. Proofpoint's Threat Intelligence and similar feeds also alert when your domain is queried from known threat infrastructure. Most importantly: your own employees are the biggest OSINT source. An out-of-office reply that says 'I'm at AWS re:Invent until Friday, contact Jane at jane@company.com' tells an attacker your email format, who the backup contact is, and when to strike.
tools_or_indicators: WAF access logs showing high-frequency scraping patterns against /about, /team, /contact pages
Google Alerts and Mention.com monitoring for company name and executive names in new pages
Proofpoint TAP (Threat and Attack Protection) or similar threat intelligence for early phishing infrastructure detection
Employee OSINT awareness training — teach staff what their public footprint looks like to an attacker

victim.title: Unknowingly Feeding the Attacker's Profile
victim.description: The employee has no idea they are being studied. Their LinkedIn profile shows their job title, team structure, what tools they use ('excited to be rolling out Salesforce'), and sometimes even internal project names. Their conference speaker bio lists what they work on. Their out-of-office message reveals email formats and who else to contact. None of this feels sensitive in isolation, but in aggregate it gives an attacker everything needed to craft a phishing email that reads like it came from someone inside the company. The victim won't remember any of this information sharing when the email arrives weeks later.
tools_or_indicators: LinkedIn profile showing job title, team, and technology stack
Out-of-office auto-replies revealing email formats and colleague names
Conference speaker bios and public presentations listing internal projects
GitHub commits with corporate email address and internal repository names

attacker.title: Crafting the Phishing Lure
attacker.description: With intelligence gathered, the attacker now builds the phishing weapon. This typically involves creating a convincing fake login page that mirrors the real one pixel-for-pixel, registering a look-alike domain (like 'micr0soft-login.com'), and drafting an email that mimics the tone, formatting, and branding of legitimate corporate communications. Advanced attackers use tools like Evilginx2, a reverse proxy tool that sits between the victim and the real login page, capturing credentials and session cookies in real time, making it effective even against multi-factor authentication.
tools_or_indicators: GoPhish, an open-source phishing framework that manages campaigns, tracks clicks, and harvests credentials
Evilginx2, a reverse proxy phishing tool that intercepts real-time authentication sessions including MFA tokens
SET (Social Engineering Toolkit), a framework for crafting social engineering attacks
Look-alike domain registration (typosquatting)
HTML/CSS cloning of legitimate login pages

defender.title: Detecting Weaponization Indicators
defender.description: Defenders can proactively detect phishing weaponization by monitoring for newly registered domains that resemble their organization's domain. Domain monitoring services and certificate transparency logs can reveal when an attacker registers a look-alike domain or obtains an SSL certificate for it. Additionally, maintaining DMARC, DKIM, and SPF records helps ensure that spoofed emails are flagged or rejected by receiving mail servers.
tools_or_indicators: Certificate Transparency log monitoring
Domain monitoring services (e.g., DNSTwist) that detect typosquatting
DMARC/DKIM/SPF email authentication configuration
Phishing URL databases and threat intelligence feeds

victim.title: Unaware of the Threat Being Built
victim.description: During this phase the victim is completely unaware that an attack is being prepared specifically for them. The phishing page may already exist, perfectly replicating the login portal they use every day, but until the email arrives in their inbox they have no indication anything is wrong. This is why proactive security awareness training matters before an attack arrives, not after. One practical habit: employees should know to hover over links before clicking and verify the domain character-by-character — 'micros0ft.com' with a zero looks identical at a glance.
tools_or_indicators: No direct indicators visible to the victim at this stage
Phishing simulation platforms (KnowBe4, Proofpoint Security Awareness) build recognition before real attacks arrive

attacker.title: Sending the Phishing Message
attacker.description: The attacker delivers the phishing email or message to the victim. To bypass email security, the attacker may send the email from a compromised legitimate account, use a trusted email service like SendGrid, or exploit misconfigured SPF/DKIM records that allow spoofed sender addresses. The email is carefully timed, often sent during busy work hours when recipients are less likely to scrutinize each message. Some attackers also use SMS (smishing) or voice calls (vishing) as alternative delivery channels.
tools_or_indicators: Compromised email accounts for sending from trusted domains
Bulk email services (SendGrid, Mailgun) abused for delivery
SPF/DKIM bypass techniques
SMS-based phishing (smishing)
QR code phishing (quishing) embedded in documents

defender.title: Filtering and Quarantining Malicious Messages
defender.description: Email security gateways are the primary defense at this stage. These systems analyze incoming messages for known phishing indicators such as suspicious URLs, mismatched sender domains, malicious attachments, and language patterns associated with social engineering. Advanced solutions use machine learning to detect zero-day phishing attempts that do not match known signatures. Defenders should also ensure that email authentication protocols (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) are strictly enforced to reject spoofed messages.
tools_or_indicators: Secure Email Gateways (Proofpoint, Mimecast, Microsoft Defender for Office 365)
SPF/DKIM/DMARC enforcement to reject spoofed senders
URL sandboxing and rewriting to analyze links before users click
Machine learning-based email threat detection

victim.title: Receiving the Phishing Message
victim.description: The phishing email lands in the victim's inbox, possibly bypassing spam filters. It looks legitimate, perhaps appearing to come from IT support, a manager, or a trusted vendor. The message creates urgency, claiming the victim's password is expiring, their account has been compromised, or an important document needs immediate review. At this moment the victim must decide whether to trust the message or investigate further, and that split-second decision is exactly what the attacker is counting on.
tools_or_indicators: Email appears in inbox with familiar branding
Urgent subject lines designed to trigger immediate action
Sender address that closely resembles a trusted contact

attacker.title: Triggering the Victim's Action
attacker.description: The exploitation phase begins the moment the victim clicks the malicious link or opens the weaponized attachment. If the lure is a fake login page, the victim's browser navigates to an attacker-controlled site that looks identical to the real one. If it is a malicious document, opening it may trigger a macro or exploit that downloads malware silently in the background. The attacker has now transitioned from passive preparation to active exploitation of the victim's trust.
tools_or_indicators: Malicious URLs redirecting to credential harvesting pages
Weaponized Office documents with VBA macros
HTML smuggling (T1027.006): the malicious payload is assembled inside the browser using JavaScript blobs or data URIs, so it never exists as a file that email scanners can inspect
Browser exploit kits that target unpatched vulnerabilities

defender.title: Blocking Exploitation Attempts
defender.description: Even if a phishing email reaches the inbox, defenders have multiple layers to prevent exploitation. Web proxies and DNS filtering can block access to known phishing domains when the victim clicks the link. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools monitor for suspicious process behavior, like a Word document spawning a PowerShell process. Disabling Office macros by default and enforcing browser isolation for untrusted URLs are highly effective preventive measures.
tools_or_indicators: DNS filtering (Cisco Umbrella, Pi-hole) to block malicious domains
Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solutions like CrowdStrike or SentinelOne
Microsoft Attack Surface Reduction rules to block Office macro execution
Web proxy solutions that inspect and block suspicious URLs

victim.title: Falling for the Deception
victim.description: The victim clicks the link or opens the attachment, genuinely believing it is legitimate. The fake login page looks exactly like the real one, or the document appears to be a normal business file. Victims are not foolish for falling for these attacks; modern phishing is extremely sophisticated and designed to exploit the way humans naturally process information under time pressure. This is why layered technical defenses are essential, because relying solely on human judgment is not enough.
tools_or_indicators: Clicking a malicious link in the email
Opening an attachment and enabling macros
Entering credentials into a fake login page

attacker.title: Capturing Credentials and Session Cookies
attacker.description: This is where reverse-proxy phishing like Evilginx2 is categorically different from a basic credential harvester. A basic fake login page captures the username and password — useful, but easily defeated by MFA. Evilginx2 sits as a real-time proxy between the victim and the actual identity provider. The victim authenticates for real, MFA included, and the legitimate session cookie is issued. Evilginx intercepts that cookie before it reaches the browser. The attacker now has a valid, post-MFA session token that can be replayed in their own browser immediately — no password needed, no MFA prompt. The victim is logged into their account normally and has no idea anything happened. The session cookie is more valuable than the password at this point.
tools_or_indicators: Evilginx2 — reverse proxy that relays real authentication and steals the resulting session cookie, bypassing TOTP and push-based MFA
Modlishka — similar reverse-proxy approach with different evasion characteristics
GoPhish — classic credential harvester, captures username and password but not session cookies
Server-side phishlet logs recording every submitted credential and intercepted token

defender.title: Detecting Stolen Sessions and Making Proxy Attacks Impossible
defender.description: The most important detection signal here is impossible travel: a user who authenticated from Stockholm at 09:00 and then from a cloud provider IP in Amsterdam at 09:02 has had their session stolen. Entra ID and Okta both surface this natively — it should be a high-priority alert, not buried in a daily report. The structural fix is FIDO2/WebAuthn (hardware security keys or passkeys). These are cryptographically bound to the origin domain. When Evilginx proxies the authentication, the browser sends the assertion to 'evilginx-proxy.com', which does not match 'login.microsoft.com' — the key refuses to sign. Proxy phishing becomes physically impossible. SMS and TOTP codes do not provide this protection. Conditional Access policies requiring compliant devices and named locations are a secondary layer that catches session replay from unexpected infrastructure.
tools_or_indicators: Impossible travel alerts in Entra ID, Okta, or Ping Identity — flag any new session from an IP geographically inconsistent with prior auth
FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys (YubiKey) or passkeys — origin-bound, defeat proxy interception entirely
Microsoft Sentinel or Splunk: alert on 'New session from IPs with no prior auth history for this user'
Dark web credential monitoring (SpyCloud, Flare) — find your credentials before the attacker uses them
Conditional Access: require compliant device + named location for cloud app access

victim.title: Fully Compromised Account, Zero Visible Indication
victim.description: The victim enters their credentials, completes their MFA challenge, and is logged into their real account as normal. Everything looks correct. The attacker now holds a valid session cookie that works like a master key — it grants full access to every application and file the victim's account can reach, for as long as the session remains valid (often hours or days). The victim's password is irrelevant; MFA is bypassed. The victim will continue working, reading emails, accessing SharePoint — completely unaware that the attacker is doing exactly the same thing in parallel. The first indication is typically an alert from the security team days later, or worse, when colleagues start receiving phishing emails sent from the victim's own account.
tools_or_indicators: Legitimate-looking redirect to real application after credential entry — nothing appears wrong
Attacker gains access to email, SharePoint, Teams, and any SSO-connected application
Session cookie valid for hours to days — all protected data accessible without triggering additional MFA

attacker.title: Maintaining Long-Term Access
attacker.description: With valid credentials or session tokens in hand, the attacker works quickly to establish persistent access that survives a password change. This may involve registering a new MFA device on the compromised account, creating OAuth application grants that provide ongoing access to email and files, setting up email forwarding rules to silently copy all incoming messages, or creating a new backdoor admin account. The attacker's goal is to ensure they do not lose access even if the phishing attack is eventually discovered.
tools_or_indicators: Registering rogue MFA devices on the compromised account
Creating OAuth app consents for persistent email/file access
Setting up hidden email forwarding or inbox rules
Creating new accounts or service principals for backup access
Installing remote access trojans (RATs) on the victim's device

defender.title: Hunting Every Persistence Mechanism the Attacker May Have Left
defender.description: Once a phishing compromise is confirmed, your first action is to revoke all active sessions for the affected account — in Entra ID this is a single PowerShell call: Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken. Then work through the persistence checklist systematically. MFA device registrations: check Entra ID audit log for 'Register security info' events in the compromise window — any device added in the last 24-48 hours that the user didn't register themselves is attacker-controlled. OAuth consents: query the app registrations and delegated permissions via Graph API or the Entra portal, looking for apps granted Mail.Read, Mail.Send, or Files.ReadWrite that the user didn't explicitly authorize. Mail rules: use Get-InboxRule in Exchange Online to list all rules for the affected mailbox — attackers routinely create 'forward to external address' or 'move to deleted items' rules to maintain surveillance. Finally, search the Entra audit log for 'Add member to role' and 'Create user' events originating from the compromised account session.
tools_or_indicators: Entra ID audit log: filter on 'Register security info', 'Consent to application', 'Add member to role' in the compromise timeframe
Exchange Online: Get-InboxRule -Mailbox user@company.com | Where-Object {$_.ForwardTo -or $_.RedirectTo}
Microsoft Graph: GET /users/{id}/oauth2PermissionGrants — enumerate all OAuth consents for the account
SOAR playbook: auto-revoke sessions, disable account, snapshot audit logs, page the analyst — all within 5 minutes of alert trigger
Revoking sessions alone is not enough — hunt persistence or the attacker walks back in

victim.title: Living with a Compromised Account
victim.description: The victim continues using their account normally, unaware that the attacker has established multiple backdoors. They may not notice the new MFA device registered on their account or the hidden email forwarding rule sending copies of their messages to an external address. Even if the victim eventually changes their password after a routine security reminder, the attacker's persistence mechanisms may still grant access. The victim only learns about the compromise when the security team notifies them, which could be days, weeks, or even months later.
tools_or_indicators: Unfamiliar MFA device registrations in account settings
Hidden inbox rules forwarding email externally
OAuth apps with broad permissions the victim did not authorize

attacks.name: Brute Force
attacks.short_description: Systematic attack that tries every possible password combination or uses common password lists to gain unauthorized access to accounts and systems.

attacker.title: Locating Login Portals and Services
attacker.description: The attacker begins by scanning the target's infrastructure to find services that require authentication. This includes web login pages, SSH servers, RDP endpoints, VPN gateways, and API endpoints. Tools like Nmap, a network scanner that probes ports and identifies running services, help the attacker map out every possible entry point. The attacker also checks for exposed admin panels (like WordPress wp-admin, phpMyAdmin, or cPanel) that are often left accessible on the public internet.
tools_or_indicators: Nmap, a network scanner that identifies open ports and running services across target systems
Shodan, a search engine that indexes internet-connected devices and reveals exposed services
Dirb or Gobuster, directory brute-forcing tools that discover hidden web paths like admin panels
Google dorking to find exposed login pages

defender.title: Reducing the Attack Surface
defender.description: Defenders should minimize the number of login portals exposed to the internet. Services like SSH and RDP should be placed behind a VPN or Zero Trust network, not directly accessible from the public internet. Web admin panels should be restricted to specific IP addresses or require VPN access. Regularly scanning your own infrastructure with the same tools attackers use helps identify accidentally exposed services before an attacker finds them.
tools_or_indicators: External attack surface management tools (Censys, Shodan monitoring)
VPN or Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) to hide internal services
Firewall rules restricting access to admin portals
Regular external penetration testing

victim.title: Using Services That May Be Exposed
victim.description: The victim, usually an employee or system administrator, uses login portals daily without realizing they are visible to the entire internet. An RDP server set up for remote work convenience, a VPN gateway with a web login, or a cloud application admin panel all represent potential brute force targets. The victim's everyday convenience of accessing these services from anywhere is exactly what makes them available for an attacker to target as well.
tools_or_indicators: Publicly accessible RDP or SSH services
Web-based email login portals
Cloud application login pages without IP restrictions

attacker.title: Building Password Lists and Username Databases
attacker.description: Before launching the actual attack, the attacker prepares their ammunition: lists of usernames and passwords to try. The famous rockyou.txt wordlist contains over 14 million real passwords leaked from a 2009 data breach and remains one of the most commonly used starting points. For targeted attacks, CeWL (Custom Word List generator) crawls the target's website to build a company-specific wordlist using words found on their pages, which often includes product names, locations, and terminology employees might use in passwords. The attacker may also harvest usernames from LinkedIn, email patterns, or previous data breaches.
tools_or_indicators: rockyou.txt, a massive password wordlist containing over 14 million real passwords from data breaches
CeWL, a tool that crawls websites to generate custom wordlists based on words found on the target's pages
SecLists, a curated collection of wordlists for usernames, passwords, URLs, and other security testing data
Credential dumps from previous data breaches found on dark web forums
Username enumeration through email harvesting or LDAP queries

defender.title: Enforcing Strong Password Policies
defender.description: The best defense against wordlist attacks is ensuring that no employee password appears in any known breach list. Modern password policies should check new passwords against databases of compromised passwords (like the Have I Been Pwned API) and reject any match. Password managers should be provided and encouraged so employees can use long, unique, randomly generated passwords without needing to remember them. Banning common password patterns like 'Company2024!' is also critical since CeWL-generated wordlists will include these variations.
tools_or_indicators: Have I Been Pwned API integration for password screening
Password managers (1Password, Bitwarden) deployed organization-wide
Azure AD / Entra ID custom banned password lists
Minimum password length of 14+ characters with complexity requirements

victim.title: Potentially Using Weak or Reused Passwords
victim.description: The victim may be using a password that is already in an attacker's wordlist without knowing it. Common patterns like a capital letter followed by a word and numbers (e.g., 'Summer2024!') feel secure but are among the first combinations attackers try. Even worse, if the victim reuses passwords across personal and work accounts, a breach at any one service exposes them everywhere. Many victims are unaware that their credentials from old breaches are freely available in compilation databases used by attackers.
tools_or_indicators: Reused passwords across multiple services
Passwords based on predictable patterns (season + year, company name + numbers)
Credentials exposed in previous data breaches

attacker.title: Launching the Attack — Online vs. Offline
attacker.description: There are two fundamentally different scenarios here, and conflating them is a common mistake. Online brute force sends authentication requests directly to the live service: Hydra fires SSH login attempts at the target server, Burp Suite Intruder replays HTTP requests to the login form. The service rate-limits or locks accounts, so the attacker must stay slow. The speed ceiling is determined by network latency and the server's rate limits — typically hundreds of attempts per minute at most. Offline hash cracking is a different game entirely. This only applies if the attacker already obtained a database dump containing password hashes — through SQL injection, a breach, or a compromised server. Now they crack those hashes locally: Hashcat on a modern GPU cluster can test 100 billion NTLM hashes per second against rockyou.txt, finishing in seconds. bcrypt at cost factor 12 slows this to roughly 10,000 hashes per second — orders of magnitude slower, which is exactly why algorithm choice matters. Credential stuffing is a third scenario: the attacker has plaintext username/password pairs from a previous breach and tries them on other services, betting on password reuse.
tools_or_indicators: Hydra (THC-Hydra) — online attack against SSH, RDP, FTP, HTTP forms; limited by target rate controls
Hashcat — offline GPU hash cracking; only applicable after obtaining hashes from a database dump or SAM file
John the Ripper — flexible offline cracker with rule-based mutations (e.g., 'password' → 'P@ssw0rd')
Burp Suite Intruder — HTTP login form brute force with customizable request templates
Credential stuffing via Sentry MBA, Snipr, or custom scripts — uses known plaintext pairs from prior breaches

defender.title: Detecting and Throttling Brute Force Attempts
defender.description: Account lockout policies and rate limiting are the first line of defense against automated attacks. After a configurable number of failed attempts (typically 5-10), the account should be temporarily locked or the source IP should be throttled. However, sophisticated attackers use 'low and slow' techniques, trying only a few passwords per account across thousands of accounts to avoid lockouts. SIEM systems should correlate failed login attempts across the entire organization to detect these distributed patterns. CAPTCHAs on login pages also slow automated tools significantly.
tools_or_indicators: Account lockout policies after consecutive failed attempts
SIEM correlation rules detecting distributed brute force patterns
CAPTCHAs or progressive delays on login pages
Fail2ban, a tool that automatically bans IP addresses after repeated failed login attempts
Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) with bot detection capabilities

victim.title: Account Under Automated Assault
victim.description: The victim's account is being bombarded with login attempts, though they typically have no idea this is happening. They might notice their account getting locked out unexpectedly, or they may receive a flurry of MFA push notifications they did not initiate (a technique called 'MFA fatigue' where attackers hope the victim eventually approves one just to stop the notifications). If the attack is distributed across many IP addresses and uses slow timing, even the account lockout mechanism may not trigger, leaving the victim completely unaware.
tools_or_indicators: Unexpected account lockouts
Multiple MFA push notifications the victim did not request
Password reset emails the victim did not initiate

attacker.title: Bypassing MFA After Cracking the Password
attacker.description: Cracking the password is only half the problem when MFA is in place. Attackers use several approaches depending on the MFA method. Push notification fatigue (MFA bombing): the attacker logs in with the valid password, which triggers an Authenticator push to the victim's phone. They repeat this dozens of times until the victim, confused or annoyed, approves one — often at 2am. Microsoft and Okta data shows this succeeds more than defenders expect. SIM swapping: the attacker social-engineers the victim's mobile carrier into transferring their phone number, then receives SMS codes. This is a telecom-layer attack, not a technical one. Pass-the-hash: if the attacker obtained an NTLM hash (rather than a cleartext password), tools like Mimikatz allow authenticating directly with the hash against NTLM-enabled services — no password, no MFA triggered, because MFA only wraps the initial authentication flow, not hash-based lateral movement.
tools_or_indicators: MFA push bombing — repeated login attempts forcing push notification fatigue; no special tooling needed beyond the cracked password
SIM swap via carrier social engineering — intercepts SMS OTP codes without any malware on victim's device
Mimikatz pass-the-hash (pth) — authenticate with NTLM hash against SMB, RDP, or WMI without triggering MFA
OAuth device code phishing — tricks victim into authorizing an attacker-controlled app via the OAuth device flow

defender.title: Not All MFA Is Equal — Know What You're Defending With
defender.description: SMS OTP is the weakest MFA: vulnerable to SIM swapping and SS7 interception. TOTP (Google Authenticator-style codes) is better but still susceptible to real-time phishing proxies. Push notifications are vulnerable to fatigue attacks — the fix is number matching, where the user must type a 2-digit number displayed on the login screen into the app before approving. This breaks automated fatigue attacks because the attacker cannot know which number to present. FIDO2/WebAuthn is the only MFA that defeats both phishing and fatigue attacks; it is cryptographically bound to the origin domain. For detection: alert on 5+ MFA denials from the same account within 10 minutes (Event ID 6273 in Windows NPS logs, or equivalent in Entra/Okta). An account being push-bombed is a password-cracked account. Treat it as a confirmed compromise, not a curiosity.
tools_or_indicators: Entra ID / Okta: alert on multiple MFA denials for same account — threshold of 5 in 10 minutes is a reasonable starting point
Enable number matching in Microsoft Authenticator (Entra ID policy: Authentication Methods → Microsoft Authenticator → Require number matching)
FIDO2 hardware keys or passkeys as MFA — origin-bound, defeats both fatigue and proxy attacks
Block legacy authentication protocols (SMTP AUTH, IMAP, POP3) that bypass MFA entirely — Conditional Access policy in Entra ID

victim.title: Facing Pressure to Approve Unauthorized Access
victim.description: If the attacker cracks the password and launches an MFA fatigue attack, the victim's phone begins buzzing repeatedly with authentication requests they did not initiate. This is deliberately annoying and disorienting. Some victims approve the request just to stop the notifications, especially if they receive them during the night. Others may think the system is malfunctioning. Victims should be trained to never approve MFA prompts they did not initiate and to report the activity immediately, as it means their password has already been compromised.
tools_or_indicators: Repeated unsolicited MFA push notifications
Phone calls from 'IT support' asking the victim to approve the prompt (social engineering combined with brute force)
Confusion about whether the prompts are system errors

attacker.title: Establishing Position and Maximising Access
attacker.description: The first thing an attacker does after a successful login is not immediately grab data — it is understand what they have. They run whoami /all to see group memberships, check whether the account has admin rights locally or on the domain, and look at what network resources are reachable. In a cloud environment they enumerate IAM roles and attached policies. If the account has no admin rights, they look for privilege escalation paths: stored credentials in config files, overpermissioned service accounts, or admin tools left running under the compromised account's context. Once they know what they have, they harvest systematically: email keyword searches for 'password', 'credentials', 'vpn', 'aws', 'secret' surface an enormous amount in most corporate mailboxes. SharePoint and OneDrive searches for finance documents, source code, and HR data. The goal before taking any action is to avoid detection — they read silently before they write.
tools_or_indicators: whoami /all, net group 'Domain Admins' /domain — first commands run to understand privilege level
Mailbox keyword search for 'password', 'credential', 'API key', 'aws_access' via OWA or Graph API
SharePoint/OneDrive search for 'confidential', 'payroll', 'source code', 'credentials' — native search leaves no special footprint
AWS CLI: aws iam get-user, aws iam list-attached-user-policies — enumerate cloud permissions post-compromise
Credential files: ~/.aws/credentials, web.config, appsettings.json, .env files — all commonly contain secrets

defender.title: Detecting Post-Compromise Activity with Behaviour Baselines
defender.description: The key insight is that attackers cannot perfectly mimic normal user behaviour. A sales representative does not run LDAP enumeration queries. A developer does not search 10,000 SharePoint files at 3am. UEBA (User and Entity Behaviour Analytics) builds a baseline for each user and alerts on deviations — the alert is not 'suspicious query' but 'this user has never done this before'. Microsoft Sentinel, Splunk UBA, and Exabeam all provide this capability. Specific detection rules that catch post-compromise activity: alert on any Microsoft Graph API call with scope Mail.Read or Files.Read initiated from a new IP; alert on more than 50 SharePoint file accesses within 5 minutes from a single account; alert on new Conditional Access policy exclusions or role assignments made outside business hours. Least privilege remains the most important structural control: an account that can only read its own mailbox and three SharePoint sites causes far less damage when compromised than one with broad access.
tools_or_indicators: Microsoft Sentinel UEBA: alert on first-time activity from new IP, device, or country for any user
Unified Audit Log (UAL) in Microsoft 365: FileAccessed, FileSyncDownloadedFull events — bulk downloads generate hundreds of events in seconds
Graph API audit: alert on new OAuth app consent or Mail.Send delegation events — attackers frequently set these for persistent access
Entra ID: alert on 'Add member to role' events originating from non-admin accounts
Least privilege review: use Entra ID Access Reviews to regularly remove unnecessary permissions

victim.title: Account Misused — the Damage Is Often Invisible Until It Isn't
victim.description: The victim's account is being used simultaneously by the attacker, who is reading emails, searching files, and potentially setting up forwarding rules so they receive future mail even after the password is reset. The victim sees nothing. If the attacker sends phishing emails from the compromised account, the victim's colleagues receive them from a trusted address and are far more likely to click — the victim's reputation and professional relationships are now an attack vector. The victim typically learns about the compromise either from the security team (best case) or from a colleague asking 'did you really just send me this?' The damage to trust in internal communications can outlast the technical compromise by months.
tools_or_indicators: Colleagues receiving unexpected emails from the victim's account with unusual attachments or requests
Account login history showing sessions from unknown IP addresses or countries
File access logs showing documents the victim never opened
Inbox rules the victim did not create, silently forwarding all mail to an external address

attacks.name: SQL Injection
attacks.short_description: Code injection technique that exploits vulnerabilities in database-connected applications to manipulate, extract, or destroy data by inserting malicious SQL statements.

attacker.title: Mapping the Web Application
attacker.description: The attacker begins by systematically exploring the target web application to understand its structure, technology stack, and potential entry points. They browse every page, submit forms, and observe how URLs and parameters change. Tools like Burp Suite, an intercepting proxy that captures and modifies every HTTP request between the browser and the server, allow the attacker to see exactly what data is being sent and how the application responds. The attacker is looking for any input field, URL parameter, or API endpoint that might interact with a backend database.
tools_or_indicators: Burp Suite, an intercepting proxy that captures, inspects, and modifies all HTTP/HTTPS traffic between the browser and server
OWASP ZAP (Zed Attack Proxy), a free security testing tool that automatically discovers web application endpoints
Wappalyzer, a browser extension that identifies the technologies (frameworks, databases, servers) a website uses
Manual browsing and spidering to discover all application pages and forms

defender.title: Hardening the Application Surface
defender.description: Defenders should assume attackers will map every endpoint and act accordingly. Removing verbose error messages that reveal database types or query structures is essential, as these details help attackers craft their injection payloads. Custom error pages should display friendly messages without technical details. HTTP response headers that reveal server software versions should be stripped. Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) can detect and block automated scanning tools, though they should be considered a supplementary defense, not a primary one.
tools_or_indicators: Custom error pages that hide technical details from users
HTTP header hardening to remove server version information
Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) like ModSecurity or Cloudflare WAF
Rate limiting on API endpoints to slow automated scanning

victim.title: Users of a Potentially Vulnerable Application
victim.description: The victims in a SQL injection attack are primarily the users whose data is stored in the application's database. During reconnaissance, these users are completely unaware that an attacker is probing the application they trust with their personal information, payment details, or login credentials. The application's developers and administrators are also victims, as their systems are being evaluated for weaknesses. Every user who has ever entered data into the application is at risk if an injection vulnerability exists.
tools_or_indicators: Personal data stored in the application's database
Trust in the application's security
No visibility into attacker reconnaissance activity

attacker.title: Finding Vulnerable Input Fields
attacker.description: The attacker now tests each input field and parameter to determine if it passes user input directly into SQL queries without proper sanitization. The simplest test is entering a single quote character (') into a field and observing whether the application returns a database error, which indicates the input is being inserted directly into a SQL query. More sophisticated tests use time-based techniques: injecting a command like 'SLEEP(5)' that causes a deliberate delay tells the attacker the injection is working even when no visible error appears. Each vulnerable parameter is a potential doorway into the entire database.
tools_or_indicators: Single quote (') test to trigger SQL syntax errors
sqlmap, an automated SQL injection detection and exploitation tool that tests parameters and identifies injection types
Boolean-based blind testing by injecting conditions like 'AND 1=1' vs 'AND 1=2' and comparing responses
Time-based blind testing using SLEEP() or WAITFOR DELAY commands
Burp Suite Scanner for automated vulnerability detection

defender.title: Preventing Injection at the Code Level
defender.description: The only truly effective defense against SQL injection is parameterized queries (also called prepared statements), where user input is always treated as data, never as executable SQL code. This means even if a user enters a SQL command as input, the database treats it as a harmless text string rather than executing it. ORMs (Object-Relational Mappers) like SQLAlchemy, Hibernate, or Entity Framework use parameterized queries by default, making them safer than writing raw SQL. Code reviews and static analysis tools should flag any instance of string concatenation in SQL queries as a critical vulnerability.
tools_or_indicators: Parameterized queries / prepared statements in all database interactions
ORM frameworks (SQLAlchemy, Hibernate, Entity Framework) that prevent raw SQL
Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools like SonarQube or Checkmarx
Code review checklists that flag string concatenation in SQL
Input validation and sanitization as a defense-in-depth measure

victim.title: Data at Risk from Vulnerable Code
victim.description: When the attacker finds an injection point, every piece of data in the connected database is potentially at risk. This includes usernames, passwords (often stored as hashes), email addresses, personal identification numbers, payment card details, medical records, and any other sensitive information the application stores. The victims whose data is in that database had no role in creating the vulnerability; it exists because of a coding error by the application's developers. This highlights why secure coding practices are so critically important.
tools_or_indicators: All data stored in the application's database is at risk
Personal information, credentials, and financial data
Data that users submitted trusting the application's security

attacker.title: Building Malicious SQL Statements
attacker.description: With a confirmed injection point, the attacker crafts SQL payloads tailored to the specific database type and injection context. UNION-based injection appends additional SELECT statements to the original query, allowing the attacker to retrieve data from any table in the database. Error-based injection deliberately triggers detailed error messages that leak data within the error output. Blind injection extracts data one bit at a time by asking the database true/false questions. The tool sqlmap automates this entire process: given a vulnerable URL, it determines the database type, discovers tables and columns, and extracts data, all without the attacker writing a single SQL statement manually.
tools_or_indicators: UNION-based payloads that combine attacker queries with legitimate ones to extract data
Error-based payloads that force the database to reveal information in error messages
Blind injection payloads that infer data through true/false responses or time delays
sqlmap with --dbs, --tables, and --dump flags for automated extraction
Manual payload crafting for WAF evasion using encoding, comments, and alternate syntax

defender.title: Detecting Injection Payloads — WAFs Are Necessary But Not Sufficient
defender.description: WAFs catch known patterns like UNION SELECT, OR 1=1, and SQL comment sequences (-- and #). A determined attacker bypasses them with URL encoding (%27 for single quote), inline comments (UN/**/ION SE/**/LECT), and database-specific alternate syntax (MySQL's backtick quoting, MSSQL's square brackets). Treat WAF blocks as signal, not as prevention: every blocked request should be logged and reviewed. Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) instruments the application at the code level — it intercepts the SQL query at the database driver layer, where it can see the fully assembled statement including any injected payload, regardless of how it was encoded at the network level. This is far more accurate. At the database layer: any query that reads from INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES or INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS is a strong indicator — no legitimate application feature needs to enumerate its own schema at runtime. Flag these in your database audit log immediately.
tools_or_indicators: WAF (ModSecurity, AWS WAF, Cloudflare) — necessary first layer; log all blocked requests for analyst review
RASP (Contrast Security, Sqreen) — intercepts SQL at the driver level; near-zero false positives compared to WAF pattern matching
Database audit log: alert on any query containing INFORMATION_SCHEMA, LOAD_FILE, INTO OUTFILE, xp_cmdshell, or SLEEP()
SIEM rule: alert on 10+ 500-error responses from the same source IP to the same endpoint within 60 seconds — classic injection probing pattern

victim.title: Database Being Queried by the Attacker
victim.description: At this stage, the attacker is effectively talking directly to the database through the application's vulnerable code. Every query the application legitimately runs can be hijacked to include the attacker's commands. The database faithfully executes these commands because they arrive through the application's trusted connection. The victims' data is being accessed, but from the database's perspective, these look like normal application queries. This is why SQL injection is so dangerous: it abuses the trust relationship between the application and its database.
tools_or_indicators: Database executing attacker-crafted queries through the application's trusted connection
No distinction between legitimate and malicious queries from the database's perspective

attacker.title: Retrieving Sensitive Data from the Database
attacker.description: The attacker systematically extracts valuable data from the database. First, they enumerate all database names, then all tables within each database, then all columns within each table, building a complete map of the data structure. They then dump the contents of high-value tables: user credentials, personal information, financial records, and administrative data. Password hashes are extracted for offline cracking. In some cases, the attacker can read files from the server's filesystem through database functions like MySQL's LOAD_FILE() or write files using INTO OUTFILE, potentially planting a web shell for direct server access.
tools_or_indicators: sqlmap --dump to extract complete table contents
INFORMATION_SCHEMA queries to enumerate database structure
MySQL LOAD_FILE() to read server files through the database
Database-specific functions to access the filesystem
Exfiltrating data through DNS queries when direct output is blocked (out-of-band extraction)

defender.title: Limiting Data Exposure and Detecting Exfiltration
defender.description: Defense in depth means that even if injection occurs, the damage should be minimized. The database user account used by the application should have the absolute minimum permissions needed, typically only SELECT, INSERT, and UPDATE on specific tables, never FILE privileges or access to system tables. Database activity monitoring solutions can alert on unusual query patterns like bulk SELECT statements against the users table or queries against INFORMATION_SCHEMA. Encrypting sensitive columns (like credit card numbers) at the database level means that even extracted data is useless without the encryption keys.
tools_or_indicators: Principle of least privilege for database user accounts
Database Activity Monitoring (DAM) solutions like Imperva or IBM Guardium
Column-level encryption for sensitive data fields
Database audit logging for all data access queries
Network monitoring for large data transfers from database servers

victim.title: Personal Data Being Stolen
victim.description: The victims' personal data is now being extracted from the database in bulk. Names, email addresses, phone numbers, physical addresses, passwords (even if hashed), and potentially financial information are being copied to the attacker's systems. The victims have no way to know this is happening. Their data was entrusted to the application, and a coding flaw has now made it accessible to an unauthorized party. This data may end up sold on dark web marketplaces, used for identity theft, or leveraged in future targeted phishing campaigns.
tools_or_indicators: Personal data being extracted without any notification to affected users
Credentials that may be cracked offline
Data that may appear on dark web marketplaces

attacker.title: Pivoting from Database Access to OS-Level Control
attacker.description: Getting query results is valuable; getting an OS shell is a different category of compromise. The path depends on the database engine. In Microsoft SQL Server: if xp_cmdshell is enabled (disabled by default since SQL Server 2005, but frequently re-enabled by lazy DBAs), a single injection payload like '; EXEC xp_cmdshell("whoami")-- gives the attacker a Windows command shell running as the SQL Server service account — commonly NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM or a local admin. From there: net user backdoor P@ss123! /add, net localgroup administrators backdoor /add, and they have a permanent local admin regardless of SQL access. In MySQL: if the database user has FILE privilege, SELECT ... INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/shell.php' writes a PHP web shell directly to the web root — the attacker then browses to shell.php and has interactive OS access. The application owner likely doesn't monitor file creation in the web root. Both paths lead to full server control: every config file, every credential, every network connection from that server.
tools_or_indicators: MSSQL xp_cmdshell — OS command execution as the SQL service account: '; EXEC xp_cmdshell('net user')--
MySQL SELECT INTO OUTFILE — write PHP web shell to web root if DB user has FILE privilege
MySQL UDF injection — load a compiled shared library to execute arbitrary C code through a SQL function call
PostgreSQL COPY TO/FROM PROGRAM — execute OS commands through the COPY command (requires superuser)
Web shell via INTO OUTFILE: <?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?> written to /var/www/html/cmd.php

defender.title: Hardening the Database to Contain a Compromise
defender.description: Assume injection will eventually succeed and design so the impact is bounded. The database service account must be a dedicated low-privilege account — not LocalSystem, not SA, not root. On SQL Server: sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell', 0 and RECONFIGURE; audit this setting weekly since admins sometimes re-enable it for 'temporary' troubleshooting and forget. On MySQL: REVOKE FILE ON *.* FROM 'appuser'@'localhost' — no application feature needs to write files, ever. The web server process and database process should run as separate users, and the database user should have no write access to web-accessible directories. Network firewall: the database server should accept connections only from the application server's IP on the database port — no direct internet access, no access to internal subnets it doesn't need. CIS Benchmarks for MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server provide a hardening checklist covering all these settings.
tools_or_indicators: SQL Server: EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell', 0; RECONFIGURE — disable and audit weekly
MySQL: SHOW GRANTS FOR 'appuser'@'localhost' — verify no FILE, SUPER, or EXECUTE privilege on production accounts
File system: verify database service account has no write access to web root (ls -la /var/www as the DB user)
Network: firewall rules allowing only app-server→database communication on the DB port; block all other inbound
CIS Benchmark hardening profiles for your specific database engine — run with Lynis or similar audit tool

victim.title: A Vulnerable Input Field Becomes a Full Server Compromise
victim.description: This phase is where the scope of what 'SQL injection' means shifts completely. It started as a database query vulnerability. If xp_cmdshell gives the attacker a SYSTEM shell, or INTO OUTFILE drops a web shell, it is now a full server compromise — not just the application's data, but every file on the server's disk, every process running on it, every network connection it has. The attacker can read the application's config files, which typically contain database connection strings, API keys, cloud credentials, and third-party service tokens. Each of those credentials is a door into another system. The server also becomes a pivot point: the attacker can scan internal networks from inside the firewall perimeter that previously blocked them. A single unparameterized SQL query can cascade from 'stolen email addresses' to 'full internal network access'.
tools_or_indicators: Application config files (web.config, .env, appsettings.json) now readable — contain credentials for every integrated service
Server acts as internal network pivot — can reach systems behind the firewall that the attacker couldn't reach from outside
Every file on the server's filesystem: SSL certificate private keys, SSH keys, backup archives
All running processes visible — can dump credentials from memory or inject into other running services

attacker.title: Stealing or Destroying the Data
attacker.description: In the final phase, the attacker either exfiltrates the stolen data for profit or destroys it for disruption. Exfiltrated databases are packaged, compressed, and transferred to attacker-controlled servers, often through encrypted channels to avoid detection. The data may be sold on dark web forums, used for identity theft, or held for ransom. Alternatively, a destructive attacker may execute DROP TABLE or DELETE commands to destroy data, or encrypt database contents and demand payment for the decryption key, combining SQL injection with a ransomware-style extortion.
tools_or_indicators: Data exfiltration through encrypted channels to attacker servers
DROP TABLE and DELETE statements to destroy data
Ransom demands threatening to publish stolen data
Dark web marketplace listings of stolen databases
DNS tunneling or HTTP-based exfiltration to bypass network controls

defender.title: Preventing Data Loss and Ensuring Recovery
defender.description: Data Loss Prevention (DLP) systems monitor network traffic for patterns that indicate sensitive data leaving the organization, such as large numbers of credit card numbers or social security numbers in outbound traffic. Network monitoring should flag unusual outbound connections from database servers, which normally should only communicate with application servers. Most critically, maintaining regular, tested, offline backups ensures that even if data is destroyed, it can be recovered. Backups should be stored separately from the production network so an attacker who compromises the database cannot also destroy the backups.
tools_or_indicators: Data Loss Prevention (DLP) systems monitoring outbound traffic
Network monitoring for unusual database server communications
Regular automated backups stored offline and immutable
Database transaction logs for forensic analysis and recovery
Incident response plans specifically for data breach scenarios

victim.title: Suffering the Consequences — Breach Notification Is Usually Too Late
victim.description: By the time users are notified of a SQL injection breach, their data has typically been in attacker hands for weeks or months. The notification itself causes immediate harm: users panic, trust in the service collapses, and the organisation faces regulatory consequences. The stolen credentials are used for credential stuffing against every other service the victim uses — their email, banking, and social media accounts are now in play. Personal data is sold on dark web forums within days and remains there indefinitely. If the attack included data destruction — DROP TABLE or DELETE without WHERE — the service goes down and users lose years of data permanently. GDPR and similar regulations require notification within 72 hours of discovering a breach, but discovering the breach in the first place often takes months if there is no database monitoring in place.
tools_or_indicators: Breach notification email — by the time this arrives, credentials have already been in attacker hands
Stolen credentials used in credential stuffing against banking, email, and social media accounts
Personal data appearing on dark web marketplaces like BreachForums within days of exfiltration
GDPR Article 33 — 72-hour notification deadline to supervisory authority; Article 34 — individual notification if high risk to rights

attacks.name: Man-in-the-Middle
attacks.short_description: Interception attack where the attacker secretly positions themselves between two communicating parties, reading and potentially altering all traffic in real time.

attacker.title: Inserting into the Communication Path
attacker.description: The attacker must first position themselves between the victim and the network gateway so that all traffic flows through their machine. The most common technique on local networks is ARP spoofing, where the attacker sends fake ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) messages to trick other devices into thinking the attacker's MAC address belongs to the router. Tools like Bettercap, a powerful network attack and monitoring framework, and Ettercap, a comprehensive suite for man-in-the-middle attacks, automate this process. On wireless networks, the attacker may set up an evil twin access point, a fake Wi-Fi hotspot with the same name as a legitimate one.
tools_or_indicators: Bettercap, a powerful Swiss Army knife for network attacks that automates ARP spoofing, DNS spoofing, and traffic interception
Ettercap, a comprehensive MITM suite that handles ARP poisoning and packet filtering on local networks
Evil twin access points that mimic legitimate Wi-Fi networks to lure victims
ARP spoofing, which tricks devices into sending traffic through the attacker by falsifying network address mappings
DHCP spoofing to become the default gateway for new network connections

defender.title: Preventing Unauthorized Network Positioning
defender.description: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on network switches validates ARP packets against a trusted binding table, preventing ARP spoofing attacks. 802.1X network access control ensures that only authenticated devices can connect to the network, making it harder for an attacker to plug in and start spoofing. For wireless networks, wireless intrusion prevention systems (WIPS) can detect evil twin access points by identifying duplicate SSIDs with different MAC addresses. Network segmentation limits the blast radius by ensuring that even if an attacker gains a position on one segment, they cannot intercept traffic on others.
tools_or_indicators: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches
802.1X Port-Based Network Access Control
Wireless Intrusion Prevention Systems (WIPS)
Network segmentation with VLANs
Static ARP entries for critical infrastructure

victim.title: Unknowingly Routing Traffic Through the Attacker
victim.description: The victim's device has been tricked into believing the attacker's machine is the network gateway. Every packet the victim sends, whether browsing the web, checking email, or accessing corporate resources, now passes through the attacker's system first. The victim's device shows no warning or indication that this has happened, because ARP spoofing operates at a network layer below what most users or even basic security tools can see. The victim continues using the network normally, completely unaware that an invisible intermediary is watching everything.
tools_or_indicators: All network traffic silently rerouted through the attacker
No visible warnings or indicators on the victim's device
Normal network performance may be maintained to avoid suspicion

attacker.title: Capturing All Network Communications
attacker.description: With all victim traffic flowing through their machine, the attacker uses packet capture tools to record and analyze every byte. Wireshark, the world's most widely used network protocol analyzer, displays the traffic in real time with detailed protocol breakdowns, allowing the attacker to see DNS queries (revealing which websites the victim visits), HTTP traffic in plain text, and metadata about encrypted connections. For targeted capture, tcpdump can filter and record specific traffic types to disk for later analysis. Any unencrypted protocol, including HTTP, FTP, Telnet, and some email protocols, exposes everything including credentials.
tools_or_indicators: Wireshark, a network protocol analyzer that captures and displays all network traffic with detailed protocol decoding
tcpdump, a command-line packet capture tool for recording specific traffic to disk
NetworkMiner, a forensic network analysis tool that extracts files and images from captured traffic
Bettercap's built-in sniffer modules for real-time credential extraction
PCredz, a tool that automatically extracts credentials from captured network traffic

defender.title: Ensuring Traffic Encryption
defender.description: The most effective defense against traffic interception is encrypting all communications. Enforcing HTTPS everywhere through HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) headers ensures browsers never send data over unencrypted HTTP. VPNs encrypt all traffic between the user's device and the VPN server, making intercepted packets unreadable even if an attacker captures them. Network monitoring tools should alert on ARP table changes, which indicate potential spoofing. DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) or DNS-over-TLS (DoT) prevents the attacker from seeing which websites users are visiting through DNS queries.
tools_or_indicators: HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) enforcing HTTPS on all connections
Corporate VPN for encrypting all traffic on untrusted networks
DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) or DNS-over-TLS (DoT) for encrypted DNS
ARP monitoring tools that alert on table changes
Network monitoring for duplicate MAC addresses

victim.title: Communications Being Silently Recorded
victim.description: Every website the victim visits, every file they download, every email they send over an unencrypted connection is being captured and recorded by the attacker. Even for encrypted HTTPS connections, the attacker can see the destination domains through DNS queries and TLS handshake metadata. If the victim accesses any service over plain HTTP, which still exists on many internal corporate applications and IoT device interfaces, their credentials and data are fully visible. The victim's browsing patterns, communication habits, and daily routines are all being cataloged.
tools_or_indicators: Unencrypted HTTP traffic fully visible to the attacker
DNS queries revealing browsing patterns
Email content exposed if using unencrypted protocols
File transfers captured including documents and images

attacker.title: Stripping Encryption from Secure Connections
attacker.description: Since most sensitive traffic is encrypted with HTTPS, the attacker attempts to downgrade these connections to plain HTTP so the content becomes readable. The tool sslstrip, created by security researcher Moxie Marlinspike, works by intercepting the redirect from HTTP to HTTPS that most websites use, keeping the victim on the unencrypted HTTP version while the attacker maintains a separate encrypted connection to the real server. The victim thinks they are browsing normally, but their browser shows 'http://' instead of 'https://', a subtle difference most users never notice. More advanced attacks may use forged SSL certificates to impersonate the target site entirely.
tools_or_indicators: sslstrip, a tool that transparently downgrades HTTPS connections to HTTP by intercepting redirect responses
Bettercap's hstshijack module that attempts to bypass HSTS protections
Forged SSL certificates generated by tools like mitmproxy
DNS spoofing combined with SSL stripping for more convincing attacks
WPAD (Web Proxy Auto-Discovery) exploitation to redirect traffic through attacker's proxy

defender.title: Enforcing Encryption That Cannot Be Downgraded
defender.description: HSTS preloading is the definitive defense against SSL stripping. When a domain is on the HSTS preload list, browsers are hardcoded to only use HTTPS for that domain, making it impossible for sslstrip to downgrade the connection because the browser will never attempt an HTTP connection in the first place. Certificate pinning in mobile apps ensures the app only trusts specific certificates, rejecting forged ones. For internal applications, certificate-based mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication makes MITM attacks detectable because the attacker cannot present the correct client certificate.
tools_or_indicators: HSTS preloading to ensure browsers never attempt HTTP connections
Certificate pinning in mobile and desktop applications
Mutual TLS (mTLS) for internal service-to-service communication
Certificate Transparency monitoring to detect forged certificates
Browser warnings for certificate errors that users should never bypass

victim.title: Browsing Without Encryption Protection
victim.description: The victim is now browsing what they believe are secure websites, but the lock icon in their browser may be missing or showing HTTP instead of HTTPS. Most users do not actively check the URL bar for the protocol, especially when focused on their work. When the victim enters their password on what appears to be their bank's website or corporate email login, the credentials travel in plain text through the attacker's machine. Modern browsers are getting better at warning users about insecure connections, but these warnings can be subtle and are often dismissed by users accustomed to clicking through security prompts.
tools_or_indicators: Missing padlock icon in browser address bar
URL showing http:// instead of https://
Browser security warnings that may be subtle or ignored
Credentials transmitted in plain text without the victim's knowledge

attacker.title: Stealing Authentication Sessions
attacker.description: Even if the attacker cannot decrypt the actual password, they can steal session tokens, which are small pieces of data (cookies) that a website sends to the browser after successful login to maintain the authenticated session. By capturing these session cookies from the traffic, the attacker can inject them into their own browser and instantly become logged in as the victim without ever knowing the password. This technique, known as session hijacking or sidejacking, is particularly effective against services that do not properly secure their session cookies with flags like Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite.
tools_or_indicators: Ferret and Hamster, tools for capturing and replaying session cookies
Cookie injection into the attacker's browser using browser developer tools
Bettercap's cookie sniffer module for real-time session token capture
Wireshark filters targeting HTTP Cookie headers in captured traffic

defender.title: Protecting Session Integrity
defender.description: Session cookies must be configured with security flags: 'Secure' ensures cookies are only sent over HTTPS, 'HttpOnly' prevents JavaScript from reading them (defending against XSS-based theft), and 'SameSite' restricts cross-origin requests. Sessions should be bound to the client's IP address and user agent, so stolen cookies fail when used from a different machine. Short session lifetimes and re-authentication for sensitive actions (like changing passwords or transferring money) limit the damage from a hijacked session. Token rotation, where the session ID changes after each request, makes captured tokens quickly obsolete.
tools_or_indicators: Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite cookie flags on all session cookies
Session binding to IP address and user agent
Short session timeouts requiring frequent re-authentication
Token rotation to invalidate captured session IDs
Re-authentication requirements for sensitive operations

victim.title: Active Session Stolen by the Attacker
victim.description: The victim is logged into their email, banking, or corporate application, and their active session has just been stolen. The attacker can now perform any action the victim can: read emails, transfer funds, access confidential documents, or change account settings. The victim may remain logged in simultaneously with the attacker, noticing nothing unusual unless the service detects concurrent sessions from different locations. Some victims only discover the hijacking when they notice unauthorized transactions, sent messages they did not write, or settings they did not change.
tools_or_indicators: Attacker accessing the victim's accounts simultaneously
Unauthorized actions performed using the victim's session
Possible concurrent session alerts from security-aware services

attacker.title: Altering Communications in Transit
attacker.description: Beyond passive eavesdropping, the attacker can actively modify data as it passes through their machine. This could mean changing the recipient account number in a wire transfer instruction, injecting malicious JavaScript into web pages the victim is viewing, modifying DNS responses to redirect the victim to fake websites, or altering email contents before they reach the recipient. Bettercap's proxy modules allow the attacker to write custom scripts that automatically modify specific content in real time. This active manipulation is what elevates a man-in-the-middle attack from surveillance to direct harm.
tools_or_indicators: Bettercap proxy modules for real-time content modification
mitmproxy, a scriptable HTTPS proxy that allows attackers to modify requests and responses programmatically
DNS spoofing to redirect victims to attacker-controlled websites
JavaScript injection into unencrypted web pages
Email content modification before delivery

defender.title: Ensuring Data Integrity
defender.description: End-to-end encryption ensures that even a positioned attacker cannot read or modify the actual message content, only the sender and recipient can decrypt it. Digital signatures on emails (using S/MIME or PGP) allow recipients to verify that the message was not altered in transit and truly came from the stated sender. For financial transactions, out-of-band verification (like confirming account details via phone call) prevents manipulation of payment instructions. Content Security Policy (CSP) headers prevent injected JavaScript from executing in the browser.
tools_or_indicators: End-to-end encryption for messaging and email
S/MIME or PGP digital signatures for email integrity verification
Out-of-band verification for high-value transactions
Content Security Policy (CSP) headers preventing script injection
Subresource Integrity (SRI) tags verifying loaded resources

victim.title: Receiving Altered Information Without Knowing
victim.description: The victim is now receiving modified data and has no way to distinguish it from legitimate content. A web page may contain injected malicious code, an email may have altered instructions, or a financial transaction may have been redirected to a different account. The victim acts on this false information in good faith, potentially transferring money to the wrong account, downloading malware from an injected link, or making decisions based on falsified data. This manipulation of trust in digital communications represents one of the most dangerous aspects of MITM attacks.
tools_or_indicators: Altered web page content including injected scripts or modified text
Modified financial instructions with changed account numbers
Fake DNS responses leading to impersonation websites

attacker.title: Removing Evidence of the Attack
attacker.description: After extracting valuable data or completing their manipulation, the attacker carefully removes all traces of their presence. This means stopping the ARP spoofing to restore normal network routing, deleting any packet capture files stored locally, clearing logs on any systems they accessed, and restoring the network's ARP tables to their legitimate state. A skilled attacker ensures that the network returns to its normal state so seamlessly that neither users nor administrators ever realize an interception occurred. The stolen data and credentials are securely transferred to the attacker's infrastructure for later use.
tools_or_indicators: Stopping ARP spoofing to restore legitimate network routing
Clearing packet capture files and local logs
Restoring ARP tables to normal state
Secure exfiltration of captured data to external infrastructure
Timestomping, altering file timestamps to hide when attack tools were used

defender.title: Preserving Forensic Evidence
defender.description: Defenders should implement centralized logging where copies of all network and system logs are sent to a separate, hardened SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) system that the attacker cannot access. Network flow data (NetFlow/IPFIX) records connection metadata even after the actual traffic is gone, providing evidence of unusual traffic patterns. ARP table monitoring with historical logging can reveal past spoofing even after the attacker stops. Retaining DHCP logs, switch port logs, and wireless access point associations helps forensic investigators reconstruct who was connected where and when.
tools_or_indicators: Centralized SIEM logging to a hardened, separate system
NetFlow/IPFIX records of all network connections
ARP table change logging and historical records
DHCP and switch port access logs
Wireless access point association logs

victim.title: Unaware the Attack Ever Happened
victim.description: Once the attacker cleans up, the victim's network connection returns to normal with no trace of the interception. The victim has no indication that their passwords were captured, their sessions were hijacked, or their communications were modified. Any consequences of the attack, such as unauthorized account access or fraudulent transactions, may not surface for days or weeks. The victim may never connect these later incidents back to the MITM attack, especially if the attacker used the stolen credentials gradually and carefully to avoid triggering security alerts.
tools_or_indicators: No residual indicators visible to the victim
Delayed consequences that are hard to trace back to the attack
Stolen credentials used gradually to avoid detection

attacks.name: Ransomware
attacks.short_description: Devastating malware attack that encrypts the victim's files and demands payment for decryption, often spreading laterally across entire networks.

attacker.title: Gaining the First Foothold
attacker.description: Ransomware operators gain initial access to the target network through one of several common entry vectors. Phishing emails with malicious attachments remain the most prevalent method, followed by exploiting exposed Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) services that are either unpatched or protected with weak passwords. Some groups purchase access from Initial Access Brokers (IABs), specialized cybercriminals who compromise organizations and sell the access to the highest bidder. Exploiting VPN vulnerabilities and unpatched public-facing servers are also common entry points, particularly for enterprise-targeted ransomware operations.
tools_or_indicators: Phishing emails with macro-enabled documents or malicious links
Exposed RDP services with weak or compromised credentials
Initial Access Brokers (IABs) selling pre-established network access on dark web forums
Exploitation of unpatched VPN appliances (e.g., Fortinet, Pulse Secure vulnerabilities)
Compromised valid credentials purchased from dark web marketplaces

defender.title: Blocking Initial Entry Points
defender.description: Defenders must secure every potential entry point since ransomware operators only need one to succeed. RDP should never be directly exposed to the internet; it should be accessible only through VPN or a Zero Trust solution with MFA. Email security gateways should block executable attachments and scan documents for malicious macros. All public-facing systems, especially VPN appliances and web servers, must be patched promptly since ransomware groups actively scan for newly disclosed vulnerabilities. Regular external penetration testing helps identify overlooked exposure before attackers do.
tools_or_indicators: VPN or Zero Trust access replacing direct RDP exposure
Email security gateways blocking malicious attachments
Rapid patching program for all public-facing systems
External attack surface monitoring
Dark web monitoring for compromised credentials

victim.title: The Organization Under Initial Attack
victim.description: A single employee clicking a phishing link or a forgotten RDP server with a weak password is all it takes for the ransomware operation to begin. At this point, the organization has no idea an attacker is inside. The compromised machine, whether it belongs to an executive, an intern, or is a neglected server in the corner of a data center, becomes the staging ground for everything that follows. The entire attack timeline from this point to encryption can be as short as a few hours or span several weeks, depending on the attacker's methodology.
tools_or_indicators: A single compromised endpoint serving as the attacker's entry point
No immediate visible indicators to the organization
The initial compromise may have occurred through routine employee actions

attacker.title: Setting Up Command and Control
attacker.description: Once inside, the attacker installs a command and control (C2) implant that maintains persistent communication with their infrastructure. Cobalt Strike, originally designed as a legitimate penetration testing tool, is the most widely used C2 framework by ransomware groups because its 'beacons' blend in with normal network traffic by communicating over HTTPS. Other popular C2 frameworks include Sliver (an open-source alternative) and Brute Ratel (designed specifically to evade EDR solutions). The implant phones home at regular intervals, allowing the attacker to remotely execute commands, upload tools, and download stolen data.
tools_or_indicators: Cobalt Strike, a commercial penetration testing tool widely abused by ransomware groups for its stealthy C2 beacons
Sliver, an open-source C2 framework that generates unique implants to evade signature detection
Brute Ratel C4, a C2 framework specifically designed to bypass endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools
Living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins) like PowerShell and certutil used to download additional tools
Scheduled tasks or registry run keys for persistence across reboots

defender.title: Detecting C2 Communications
defender.description: Network Detection and Response (NDR) solutions analyze network traffic patterns to identify C2 beacons, which typically show regular intervals between communications (known as 'beaconing behavior'). EDR tools on endpoints monitor for suspicious process chains, like a Word document spawning PowerShell which then connects to an external server. Blocking known-bad IP addresses and domains through threat intelligence feeds catches some C2 traffic, but advanced operators use cloud-hosted redirectors that change frequently. Application whitelisting prevents unauthorized executables from running in the first place.
tools_or_indicators: Network Detection and Response (NDR) solutions identifying beaconing patterns
EDR tools monitoring for suspicious process execution chains
Threat intelligence feeds blocking known C2 infrastructure
Application whitelisting (AppLocker, Windows Defender Application Control)
DNS monitoring for suspicious domain lookups

victim.title: A Compromised Machine Calling Home
victim.description: One of the organization's machines is now silently communicating with the attacker's infrastructure. The C2 implant is designed to be invisible, hiding among normal network traffic and using encrypted channels that look like regular HTTPS browsing. The affected machine continues to function normally for its user. Meanwhile, the attacker has established a reliable tunnel into the network that gives them remote access equivalent to sitting at the keyboard.
