This is the last point where detection and response can prevent the catastrophic phases that follow.
tools_or_indicators: Unusual outbound connections to unfamiliar domains
Periodic network beaconing at regular intervals
New scheduled tasks or services that the user did not create

attacker.title: Gaining Administrative Control
attacker.description: The initial compromised account is usually a standard user without the administrative privileges needed to execute the full ransomware attack. The attacker uses Mimikatz, a tool that extracts plaintext passwords, password hashes, and Kerberos tickets from Windows memory, to harvest credentials from the compromised machine. They exploit unpatched local vulnerabilities like PrintNightmare or misconfigured services to elevate to local administrator. From there, they target domain credentials, looking for service accounts with excessive privileges, cached domain admin credentials, or Kerberos ticket-granting tickets that can be abused in Golden Ticket attacks.
tools_or_indicators: Mimikatz, a tool that extracts passwords, hashes, and authentication tokens directly from Windows memory
PrintNightmare and other local privilege escalation exploits
Kerberoasting, an attack that requests Kerberos service tickets and cracks them offline to reveal service account passwords
Token impersonation to assume the identity of higher-privileged processes
Exploiting misconfigured Group Policy Preferences that store encrypted passwords

defender.title: Limiting Privilege Escalation Opportunities
defender.description: Implementing the principle of least privilege drastically limits privilege escalation opportunities. Local administrator passwords should be unique per machine using LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution), which automatically rotates and secures local admin passwords. Credential Guard on Windows prevents Mimikatz from reading credentials from memory. Service accounts should use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs) with automatically rotated, complex passwords that resist Kerberoasting. Promptly patching known privilege escalation vulnerabilities and monitoring for tools like Mimikatz through EDR are essential defensive measures.
tools_or_indicators: LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) for unique local admin passwords
Windows Credential Guard to protect credentials in memory
Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs) with automatic password rotation
Rapid patching of privilege escalation vulnerabilities
EDR detection rules for Mimikatz and similar credential dumping tools

victim.title: Administrative Credentials Being Stolen
victim.description: The organization's most powerful credentials are now being harvested by the attacker. Domain administrator accounts, service accounts with broad access, and backup operator accounts are all targets. Each credential the attacker captures expands their control over the network. IT administrators who have logged into the initially compromised machine may have left cached credentials that the attacker can now extract. The organization's Active Directory, which controls access to everything, is being systematically compromised from the inside.
tools_or_indicators: Domain admin credentials extracted from memory
Service account passwords cracked through Kerberoasting
Cached credentials from previous admin logins being harvested

attacker.title: Mapping the Entire Network
attacker.description: With elevated privileges, the attacker conducts thorough reconnaissance of the internal network to understand its structure, identify high-value targets, and plan the encryption strategy. Active Directory is queried using tools like BloodHound, which maps trust relationships and attack paths to identify the shortest route to domain admin. Network scanning with tools like Advanced IP Scanner reveals all connected systems, file servers, backup servers, and database servers. The attacker specifically looks for backup infrastructure because destroying backups before encryption ensures the victim cannot recover without paying the ransom.
tools_or_indicators: BloodHound, a tool that maps Active Directory relationships and identifies attack paths to high-value targets
Advanced IP Scanner and Nmap for discovering all network-connected systems
PowerView, a PowerShell tool for querying Active Directory objects, permissions, and group memberships
Net commands (net view, net group) for enumerating shares and domain groups
Identifying backup servers, NAS devices, and cloud backup solutions for later destruction

defender.title: Detecting Internal Reconnaissance
defender.description: Internal network scanning and Active Directory enumeration generate distinctive patterns that security monitoring should detect. Unusual LDAP queries, especially those requesting information about all computers, all users, or all group memberships, are a strong indicator of attacker reconnaissance. Honeypots, fake systems placed on the network that no legitimate user should ever access, provide high-confidence alerts when an attacker's scanning touches them. Monitoring for BloodHound's characteristic SharpHound data collection and large LDAP queries helps catch this phase before the attacker completes their network map.
tools_or_indicators: SIEM alerts on unusual LDAP enumeration queries
Honeypots and honey accounts that trigger alerts when accessed
Network monitoring for broad port scanning from internal hosts
Detection of SharpHound (BloodHound's data collector) execution
Alerts on enumeration of backup infrastructure

victim.title: Network Being Mapped by the Attacker
victim.description: The attacker now has a complete map of the organization's network: every server, every workstation, every file share, every database, and critically, every backup system. They know which systems hold the most valuable data, which accounts have the most access, and where the organization's recovery capabilities reside. This level of internal knowledge, often rivaling what the IT department itself knows, is what makes the coming encryption so devastating. The attacker has identified every target they need to hit and every recovery mechanism they need to neutralize.
tools_or_indicators: Complete internal network topology mapped by the attacker
All file servers, databases, and backup systems identified
Active Directory structure and trust relationships documented

attacker.title: Spreading Across the Network
attacker.description: Using harvested domain administrator credentials, the attacker moves from the initially compromised machine to other systems throughout the network. PsExec, a legitimate Microsoft tool for remote command execution, allows the attacker to run commands on any machine they have admin credentials for. Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) and PowerShell Remoting provide additional remote execution capabilities that blend in with normal administrative activity. The attacker deploys their tools to file servers, domain controllers, and backup servers, positioning for maximum impact. RDP may be used for hands-on interaction with critical systems.
tools_or_indicators: PsExec, a Microsoft Sysinternals tool abused for remote command execution across the network
WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) for stealthy remote command execution
PowerShell Remoting for executing scripts on remote machines
RDP connections to critical servers for interactive access
Deploying C2 beacons on multiple machines for redundant access

defender.title: Restricting Lateral Movement
defender.description: Network segmentation is the most effective defense against lateral movement. Critical systems like domain controllers, backup servers, and financial systems should be in separate network segments with strict access controls. Implementing a tiered administration model ensures that domain admin accounts are only used on domain controllers, never on regular workstations where they could be captured. Disabling unnecessary remote access protocols (like WMI and PowerShell Remoting on workstations) reduces the attacker's options. EDR solutions should alert on unusual remote execution patterns, like PsExec being used from a workstation that has never used it before.
tools_or_indicators: Network segmentation isolating critical systems
Tiered administration model for privileged accounts
Disabling WMI and PowerShell Remoting where not needed
EDR alerts on unusual PsExec or remote execution activity
Just-In-Time (JIT) access requiring approval for admin privileges

victim.title: Attacker Spreading Through the Organization
victim.description: The attacker is now present on numerous systems throughout the network. File servers that store critical business documents, database servers with customer data, email servers with years of communication, and backup systems that represent the organization's recovery lifeline are all under the attacker's control. The IT team may notice occasional anomalies, a service restarting unexpectedly, a brief spike in CPU usage, but these signs are subtle and easily dismissed as normal operational issues. The organization is now just one command away from catastrophe.
tools_or_indicators: Attacker present on multiple critical systems simultaneously
Subtle anomalies in system behavior that may go unnoticed
Backup systems compromised and ready to be destroyed

attacker.title: Stealing Data Before Encryption (Double Extortion)
attacker.description: Modern ransomware operations practice 'double extortion': they steal sensitive data before encrypting it, giving them two forms of leverage. If the victim has backups and can recover from encryption, the attacker threatens to publish the stolen data publicly, causing reputational damage, regulatory fines, and legal liability. The attacker identifies and collects the most damaging data: financial records, customer databases, intellectual property, legal documents, and employee personal information. This data is compressed and exfiltrated to attacker-controlled servers, often using legitimate cloud storage services like Mega.nz or rclone to avoid detection.
tools_or_indicators: rclone, a command-line program for syncing files to cloud storage, abused for data exfiltration to services like Mega.nz
7-Zip or WinRAR for compressing stolen data before exfiltration
Legitimate cloud storage services abused as exfiltration destinations
FTP or SFTP transfers to attacker infrastructure
Data staged in temporary directories before bulk transfer

defender.title: Detecting Data Theft in Progress
defender.description: Data Loss Prevention (DLP) systems should alert on large volumes of data being transferred to external destinations, especially cloud storage services and unknown IP addresses. Monitoring for unusual use of compression tools like 7-Zip or rclone on servers that normally do not use them is a strong indicator. Network monitoring should flag large outbound transfers from file servers, especially outside business hours. Even if the ransomware encryption is ultimately successful, detecting exfiltration early may allow defenders to understand what was stolen and prepare for the extortion component.
tools_or_indicators: DLP systems monitoring for bulk data transfers
Network monitoring for unusual outbound traffic volumes
Alerts on rclone, 7-Zip, or WinRAR execution on servers
Cloud access security broker (CASB) detecting uploads to unauthorized cloud services
NetFlow analysis identifying large data flows to external IPs

victim.title: Sensitive Data Being Stolen
victim.description: The organization's most sensitive data is being copied to attacker-controlled servers. Customer records, financial data, trade secrets, employee personal information, and confidential business communications are all being exfiltrated. This theft represents a separate crisis from the coming encryption: even if the organization successfully recovers all its data from backups, the stolen information can be published, sold, or used for further extortion. Many organizations that refuse to pay the ransom for decryption end up negotiating to prevent data publication, giving the attacker leverage regardless of the victim's backup strategy.
tools_or_indicators: Sensitive data being copied to external attacker infrastructure
Customer records, financial data, and intellectual property at risk
Data theft creating leverage independent of the encryption attack

attacker.title: Encrypting Everything and Demanding Payment
attacker.description: With data exfiltrated and backup systems already compromised, the attacker executes the encryption simultaneously across all targeted systems. The ransomware uses strong encryption (typically AES-256 combined with RSA for key management) that is mathematically impossible to break without the decryption key. Shadow copies and local backups are deleted first using commands like 'vssadmin delete shadows /all' to prevent easy recovery. Each encrypted file receives a new extension (like .locked, .encrypted, or a random string), and a ransom note is placed on every desktop and in every directory, providing instructions for contacting the attacker and paying the ransom, typically in Bitcoin or Monero cryptocurrency.
tools_or_indicators: AES-256 encryption with RSA key wrapping making decryption without the key impossible
vssadmin delete shadows /all to destroy Windows Volume Shadow Copies
bcdedit commands to disable Windows recovery boot options
Ransom notes (README.txt or similar) placed in every directory
Encryption executed simultaneously across hundreds of machines via Group Policy or PsExec
Tor-based payment portal for anonymous ransom negotiations

defender.title: Responding to Active Encryption
defender.description: Once encryption begins, speed is everything. Network isolation should be triggered immediately: disconnecting affected segments from the network can prevent the ransomware from reaching systems it has not yet encrypted. Pre-planned incident response procedures should activate, including contacting law enforcement, engaging a specialized incident response firm, and notifying the organization's cyber insurance carrier. Immutable, offline backups that the attacker could not reach are the primary recovery mechanism. Organizations should never assume they need to pay; many ransomware variants have known decryptors, and law enforcement operations sometimes recover decryption keys.
tools_or_indicators: Network isolation to contain the encryption spread
Immutable offline backups for recovery without paying
Incident response retainer with a specialized IR firm
Law enforcement notification (FBI IC3, local CERT)
No More Ransom project (nomoreransom.org) for free decryptors
Cyber insurance activation for incident response support

victim.title: Organization Crippled by Encryption
victim.description: The organization wakes up to discover that every file server, every workstation, every database, and every application has been encrypted and is completely unusable. Operations grind to a halt. Employees cannot access their files, customers cannot be served, and critical business processes stop. A ransom note demands payment, often hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars in cryptocurrency, with a deadline after which the price increases or the stolen data is published. The organization faces an agonizing decision: pay the ransom with no guarantee of recovery, or attempt to rebuild from backups, which could take weeks and may not be complete if backups were also compromised.
tools_or_indicators: All files encrypted with new file extensions
Ransom notes on every desktop and in every folder
Complete operational shutdown affecting all business functions
Ransom demands ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars
Threat of publishing stolen data if ransom is not paid

attacks.name: Lateral Movement
attacks.short_description: Post-compromise technique where attackers move through a network from one system to another, escalating privileges and expanding their access to reach high-value targets.

attacker.title: Establishing the First Foothold
attacker.description: Lateral movement begins after an attacker has already gained access to a single machine in the target network through any initial access vector, whether phishing, exploiting a vulnerability, or using stolen credentials. This first compromised machine is often a regular employee workstation with limited privileges, not the attacker's ultimate target. The attacker stabilizes their access by deploying a persistent backdoor and begins evaluating the network context of the compromised machine: what domain it belongs to, what network segment it sits on, what users have logged into it, and what other systems it can reach.
tools_or_indicators: Persistent backdoor installed via scheduled task, registry key, or startup folder
Initial foothold typically on a standard employee workstation
Reconnaissance commands: whoami, ipconfig, systeminfo, net user
C2 implant established for reliable remote access

defender.title: Detecting the Initial Compromise Early
defender.description: The best defense against lateral movement is detecting and containing the initial compromise before the attacker can spread. EDR solutions on every endpoint monitor for suspicious process execution, unauthorized persistence mechanisms, and C2 communications. The earlier this first foothold is detected, the less damage occurs. Security teams should prioritize alerts involving new scheduled tasks, unusual PowerShell execution, and processes making outbound connections to unfamiliar destinations. Rapid containment of a single compromised machine prevents the exponentially worse scenario of an attacker moving freely through the network.
tools_or_indicators: EDR on all endpoints detecting suspicious process chains
SIEM correlation of authentication events across the network
Alerts on new scheduled tasks and unusual persistence mechanisms
Network monitoring for C2 beacon patterns

victim.title: One Machine Compromised, Many at Risk
victim.description: A single employee's workstation has been compromised, and from the organization's perspective, every system that workstation can communicate with is now at risk. The affected employee continues working normally, unaware that their machine is now a staging platform for a much larger attack. The trust relationships that make the corporate network function, shared file servers, single sign-on, domain authentication, are about to be exploited. What seems like an isolated endpoint compromise is actually the beginning of a network-wide threat.
tools_or_indicators: Single workstation serving as the attacker's network entry point
All systems reachable from that workstation are at risk
Normal user activity masking the attacker's presence

attacker.title: Mapping the Internal Network and Domain
attacker.description: From the initial foothold, the attacker maps the internal network to identify high-value targets and plan their movement path. BloodHound, a tool that visualizes Active Directory trust relationships and attack paths, is invaluable here because it can automatically identify the shortest path from the current compromised user to domain admin access. PowerView, a PowerShell-based Active Directory enumeration tool, queries group memberships, computer objects, and access control lists without triggering most security alerts because it uses native Windows protocols. The attacker identifies where domain admins log in, which servers hold sensitive data, and what trust relationships exist between domains.
tools_or_indicators: BloodHound with SharpHound collector, which maps Active Directory attack paths and identifies the fastest route to domain admin
PowerView, a PowerShell tool that enumerates Active Directory objects, permissions, and group memberships using native LDAP queries
ADRecon, a tool that generates detailed Active Directory reports for attackers to analyze offline
Nmap or Advanced IP Scanner for network host discovery
Net commands: net group 'Domain Admins' /domain, net view, net share

defender.title: Detecting Internal Enumeration Activity
defender.description: Monitoring Active Directory query patterns is crucial for detecting internal reconnaissance. BloodHound's SharpHound collector generates a distinctive burst of LDAP queries that request information about all users, groups, computers, and sessions in the domain, a pattern no legitimate application typically produces. Deploying honeypot accounts (fake accounts that appear to be high-value targets like service accounts or admins) provides high-confidence alerting because any authentication attempt against them is guaranteed to be malicious. Monitoring for unusual net.exe and PowerShell usage on workstations helps catch manual enumeration.
tools_or_indicators: LDAP query monitoring for bulk enumeration patterns
Honeypot accounts and computers that alert when queried or accessed
PowerShell script block logging to capture enumeration commands
Detection rules for SharpHound data collection patterns
Monitoring net.exe usage on non-admin workstations

victim.title: Network Architecture Being Analyzed
victim.description: The attacker now understands the organization's network better than most of its own employees do. They know which servers hold the company's most critical data, which accounts have the most powerful access, and exactly which path through the network leads from their current position to their ultimate target. Active Directory, the backbone of Windows enterprise networks that manages authentication and authorization for every user and computer, has revealed its complete structure to the attacker. Every trust relationship, every group membership, and every administrative delegation is now known.
tools_or_indicators: Complete Active Directory structure mapped by the attacker
High-value targets identified including domain controllers and file servers
Administrative account locations and login patterns discovered

attacker.title: Dumping Credentials from Memory and Storage
attacker.description: The attacker harvests credentials from the compromised machine using multiple techniques. Mimikatz extracts plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets directly from the LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service) process memory, which Windows uses to manage user authentication. LSASS contains credentials for every user who has logged into the machine, so a compromised workstation where an IT admin once logged in to troubleshoot yields their domain admin credentials. The attacker also searches for credentials in configuration files, scripts, browser saved passwords, and Windows Credential Manager, often finding service account passwords, database connection strings, and API keys.
tools_or_indicators: Mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords to dump all credentials from LSASS memory
LSASS memory dump using procdump or comsvcs.dll for offline extraction
Dumping SAM database for local account hashes
Searching files for stored passwords (findstr /si password *.txt *.xml *.config)
LaZagne, a tool that recovers passwords stored by dozens of applications including browsers, email clients, and databases

defender.title: Protecting Credentials from Extraction
defender.description: Windows Credential Guard uses virtualization-based security to isolate the LSASS process so that even administrator-level code cannot read credentials from it, making Mimikatz ineffective on protected systems. Enabling LSA protection (RunAsPPL) adds another layer that prevents unauthorized processes from accessing LSASS memory. Tiered administration ensures that privileged accounts never log into regular workstations, eliminating the scenario where admin credentials are cached on compromised machines. Regular credential rotation for service accounts and implementing gMSAs (Group Managed Service Accounts) limits the window of usefulness for any stolen credentials.
tools_or_indicators: Windows Credential Guard isolating LSASS from unauthorized access
LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) preventing LSASS memory dumps
Tiered administration model keeping admin credentials off workstations
gMSAs for automatic service account password rotation
Monitoring for LSASS access attempts through EDR

victim.title: Credentials Harvested from the Network
victim.description: Every user who has ever logged into the compromised machine has potentially had their credentials stolen. This includes not just the machine's primary user, but also IT support staff who logged in remotely, service accounts that run scheduled tasks, and any administrator who used the machine for troubleshooting. The most dangerous scenario occurs when a domain admin's credentials are found, because that single set of credentials grants the attacker unlimited access to every system in the domain. Many organizations discover during incident response that a single compromised workstation yielded credentials for dozens of accounts.
tools_or_indicators: All accounts that logged into the compromised machine have exposed credentials
IT support and admin credentials from past troubleshooting sessions
Service account credentials cached on the machine

attacker.title: Moving to Other Machines Using Stolen Credentials
attacker.description: Armed with harvested credentials, the attacker begins moving to other systems on the network. PsExec allows the attacker to remotely execute commands on any machine where they have admin credentials, essentially giving them a command prompt on the target system. WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) and WinRM (Windows Remote Management) provide similar remote execution capabilities but may be less likely to trigger security alerts because they are commonly used by legitimate administrators. Pass-the-hash attacks allow the attacker to authenticate using stolen NTLM hashes without knowing the actual password, and Pass-the-ticket attacks abuse stolen Kerberos tickets to access services as the ticket's owner.
tools_or_indicators: PsExec for remote command execution using admin credentials on target systems
WMI (wmic /node:target process call create) for stealthy remote execution
WinRM/PowerShell Remoting for executing scripts on remote machines
Pass-the-hash using stolen NTLM hashes to authenticate without passwords
Pass-the-ticket using stolen Kerberos tickets to impersonate users
RDP for interactive access to critical servers

defender.title: Blocking and Detecting Lateral Movement
defender.description: Microsegmentation restricts network communication between systems so that workstations cannot directly connect to each other or to sensitive servers except through approved paths. This dramatically limits lateral movement options. Monitoring for PsExec usage, especially from non-admin workstations, provides high-fidelity alerting. Windows Event Log forwarding should capture Event IDs 4624 (logon) and 4648 (explicit credential use) and correlate them to detect a single set of credentials being used across many machines in a short time. Disabling NTLM authentication where possible forces Kerberos-only authentication, making pass-the-hash attacks ineffective.
tools_or_indicators: Microsegmentation restricting workstation-to-workstation communication
Windows Event Log monitoring for Event IDs 4624 and 4648
PsExec detection through Sysmon and EDR
Disabling NTLM to prevent pass-the-hash attacks
Behavioral analytics detecting one account accessing many systems rapidly

victim.title: Attacker Spreading Through the Network
victim.description: The attacker is now hopping from system to system, each new machine providing additional credentials, data, and access to more of the network. What began as a single compromised workstation has expanded to file servers, database servers, and potentially domain controllers. Each pivot looks like legitimate administrative activity because the attacker is using real credentials and authorized tools like PsExec and WMI. The organization's centralized authentication system, which was designed for convenience and efficiency, is being turned against it, allowing a single compromised credential to unlock dozens of systems.
tools_or_indicators: Attacker present on multiple systems across the network
Legitimate tools being used with stolen credentials
Each compromised system yielding more credentials for further movement

attacker.title: Reaching Domain Administrator Access
attacker.description: The attacker's ultimate goal in lateral movement is reaching domain administrator access, which provides complete control over the entire Active Directory environment. If they have not already obtained domain admin credentials through Mimikatz, they pursue advanced attacks: DCSync uses the domain replication protocol to request password hashes for any account directly from a domain controller, including the krbtgt account needed for Golden Ticket attacks. A Golden Ticket, forged using the krbtgt hash, is a Kerberos ticket-granting ticket that gives the attacker unlimited access to any resource in the domain for as long as they want, persisting even through password resets.
tools_or_indicators: DCSync attack using Mimikatz to replicate credentials directly from domain controllers
Golden Ticket attack forging Kerberos tickets using the stolen krbtgt hash
Silver Ticket attacks forging service tickets for specific services
Exploiting Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) for privilege escalation
Abusing Group Policy to push malicious configurations domain-wide

defender.title: Protecting Domain Administrator Access
defender.description: Domain admin accounts should be protected with extreme measures: they should only be used on domain controllers accessed through Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs), never for routine administration. The krbtgt account password should be rotated twice regularly (twice because Kerberos remembers the current and previous password) to invalidate any Golden Tickets. Monitoring for DCSync activity is critical: the domain controller replication protocol should only be used between actual domain controllers, so any other source using it is highly suspicious. Microsoft's Advanced Threat Analytics (ATA) or Defender for Identity specifically detect these advanced Active Directory attacks.
tools_or_indicators: Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) for domain admin activities
Regular krbtgt password rotation to invalidate Golden Tickets
Microsoft Defender for Identity detecting DCSync and Golden Ticket attacks
Monitoring directory replication (DRS) protocol usage from non-DC sources
Protected Users security group for high-privilege accounts

victim.title: Complete Domain Compromise
victim.description: With domain administrator access, the attacker has achieved total control over the organization's Windows environment. They can read anyone's email, access any file share, modify any system configuration, create or delete any account, and push software to any machine through Group Policy. A Golden Ticket attack is particularly devastating because it persists even if every user password in the organization is reset; only rotating the krbtgt password (twice) invalidates it. The organization is now completely compromised, and recovery may require rebuilding Active Directory from scratch, a process that can take weeks or months.
tools_or_indicators: Attacker has unlimited access to all domain resources
Golden Tickets provide persistent access surviving password resets
Any user account can be impersonated at will
Group Policy can be used to push malware to all machines

attacker.title: Ensuring Persistent Control Across the Domain
attacker.description: With domain admin access secured, the attacker establishes multiple persistence mechanisms to maintain long-term control even if some are discovered and removed. They create additional admin accounts with innocuous names that blend in with legitimate service accounts. They install backdoors in Group Policy Objects (GPOs) that execute their payload on every machine at boot. They may compromise Active Directory Certificate Services to issue themselves certificates that provide authentication without passwords. The attacker's goal is redundancy: they want so many persistence mechanisms that removing one or even several does not eliminate their access.
tools_or_indicators: Creating backdoor admin accounts disguised as service accounts
Modifying Group Policy Objects to execute malicious payloads at boot
Compromising AD Certificate Services for certificate-based authentication persistence
DCShadow attack to inject rogue objects directly into Active Directory replication
Skeleton Key attack to create a master password that works for any account

defender.title: Detecting and Removing Domain-Wide Persistence
defender.description: Recovering from a domain-level compromise requires systematic removal of all persistence mechanisms, a process that can be more complex than rebuilding from scratch. Defenders should audit all admin accounts against a known-good baseline, review every Group Policy Object for unauthorized modifications, and check Active Directory Certificate Services for rogue certificates. Microsoft Defender for Identity provides continuous monitoring for these persistence techniques. In severe cases, the recommended recovery is to rebuild Active Directory completely using Microsoft's forest recovery guidance, rotating all credentials including krbtgt, machine accounts, and trust relationships.
tools_or_indicators: Complete audit of all administrative accounts against baselines
GPO review for unauthorized modifications
AD Certificate Services audit for rogue certificates
Microsoft Defender for Identity for continuous AD monitoring
Active Directory forest recovery procedures for complete compromise

victim.title: Organization Under Persistent Control
victim.description: The attacker has achieved domain dominance: they control the organization's entire IT infrastructure through multiple redundant backdoors. Removing the attacker at this point is extraordinarily difficult because they have embedded themselves into the core identity and management systems. The organization may be forced into a complete Active Directory rebuild, which means extended downtime, re-provisioning every user account and machine, and re-establishing all trust relationships. This represents the worst-case scenario for lateral movement: a single compromised workstation has escalated to total organizational compromise.
tools_or_indicators: Multiple hidden persistence mechanisms throughout Active Directory
Complete IT infrastructure under attacker control
Recovery requiring potential full Active Directory rebuild

attacks.name: Supply Chain Attack
attacks.short_description: Sophisticated attack that compromises a trusted vendor, software package, or update mechanism to distribute malware to all downstream users and organizations.

attacker.title: Selecting the Supply Chain Target
attacker.description: The attacker identifies a software vendor, open-source library, or update mechanism that is widely used by their intended victims. High-value targets include enterprise software vendors like SolarWinds (whose Orion platform was used by 18,000 organizations including US government agencies), popular package registries like npm (JavaScript) and PyPI (Python) where a single compromised package can affect millions of developers, and managed service providers (MSPs) whose tools have direct access to hundreds of client networks. The attacker evaluates targets based on reach (how many downstream users), access (what privileges the software has), and security posture (how easy the vendor is to compromise).
tools_or_indicators: Analyzing software bill of materials (SBOMs) to identify widely-used dependencies
Researching popular packages on npm, PyPI, and other registries
Identifying enterprise software vendors with privileged network access
Evaluating managed service providers (MSPs) that manage multiple client environments
Studying the target vendor's development and release processes

defender.title: Understanding and Managing Supply Chain Risk
defender.description: Organizations must maintain a complete inventory of all third-party software, libraries, and services they depend on, commonly called a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM). Each dependency represents a potential attack vector and should be assessed for security risk. Vendor security assessments should evaluate not just what the software does but how the vendor secures their development pipeline. Reducing the number of dependencies, pinning specific versions (rather than automatically pulling the latest), and using private package registries that mirror and scan public packages all reduce supply chain risk. The key principle is that every piece of external software you use extends your trust boundary to include that vendor's security practices.
tools_or_indicators: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) generation and management
Vendor security assessment questionnaires and audits
Private package registries mirroring and scanning public repositories
Dependency pinning to specific reviewed versions
Software Composition Analysis (SCA) tools like Snyk or Dependabot

victim.title: Trusting External Software and Vendors
victim.description: Organizations depend on hundreds or thousands of external software components, from the operating system itself to tiny open-source libraries buried deep in their application dependencies. Each dependency is built on trust: trust that the vendor's code is not malicious, that their build pipeline is secure, and that their update mechanism has not been compromised. Most organizations have no visibility into how their vendors develop and distribute software. A single compromised component anywhere in this chain of trust can provide an attacker with direct access to the organization's systems, bypassing all perimeter defenses because the malicious code arrives through a trusted channel.
tools_or_indicators: Hundreds of external software dependencies in typical enterprise environments
Automatic update mechanisms that pull new versions without review
Trust in vendor code signing and distribution infrastructure

attacker.title: Infiltrating the Development and Build Environment
attacker.description: The attacker compromises the target vendor's software development infrastructure. This could involve phishing a developer to gain access to the source code repository, compromising the CI/CD (Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment) pipeline that automatically builds and packages the software, or gaining access to the code signing certificates used to mark builds as legitimate. In the SolarWinds attack, the attackers (attributed to Russian intelligence) inserted malicious code into the build process itself so that the malicious version was compiled, signed with SolarWinds' legitimate certificate, and distributed through their normal update channels, making it virtually undetectable.
tools_or_indicators: Compromising developer accounts through phishing or credential theft
Infiltrating CI/CD pipelines (Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) to modify the build process
Stealing code signing certificates to sign malicious builds as legitimate
Inserting backdoors directly into source code repositories
Compromising build servers to inject code during compilation

defender.title: Securing the Software Development Pipeline
defender.description: Software vendors must treat their build pipeline as critical infrastructure. Implementing SLSA (Supply chain Levels for Software Artifacts) framework provides a graduated approach to build pipeline security. All source code changes should require multi-person review. Build environments should be ephemeral (created fresh for each build and destroyed afterward) to prevent persistent compromise. Code signing certificates should be stored in hardware security modules (HSMs) that require multi-party authorization. Reproducible builds, where the same source code always produces the same binary, allow independent verification that no unauthorized code was inserted during the build process.
tools_or_indicators: SLSA framework for supply chain security levels
Multi-person code review requirements for all changes
Ephemeral build environments created and destroyed for each build
Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) for code signing key protection
Reproducible builds for independent verification
Sigstore for transparent code signing

victim.title: Vendor's Build System Compromised
victim.description: The vendor that the organization trusts has had their build pipeline compromised. From this point forward, every software update the vendor produces may contain malicious code, and it will be signed with the vendor's legitimate certificate so it appears completely authentic. The downstream organizations, the ultimate victims, have no way to detect this compromise because they verify software integrity by checking the vendor's signature, and the signature is genuine. The vendor themselves may not know their pipeline is compromised for weeks or months, during which every customer who updates receives the backdoored version.
tools_or_indicators: Vendor's build pipeline producing backdoored software with legitimate signatures
No way for downstream customers to distinguish malicious builds from clean ones
Vendor potentially unaware of the compromise for extended periods

attacker.title: Inserting the Backdoor into Legitimate Code
attacker.description: The attacker carefully inserts malicious code into the legitimate software in a way that avoids detection during code review. The backdoor is typically designed to be stealthy: it may only activate under specific conditions, communicate with C2 servers using encrypted channels that mimic normal traffic, and lie dormant for a configurable period before activating to avoid immediate detection. In the SolarWinds case, the SUNBURST backdoor waited 12-14 days before activating, checked for security tools and sandboxes before running, and communicated through DNS queries that looked like normal SolarWinds telemetry. For open-source package attacks, techniques include typosquatting (publishing 'loadsh' instead of 'lodash') or dependency confusion (publishing a higher-version internal package name to a public registry).
tools_or_indicators: Dormant backdoors that activate only after a delay period
C2 communication disguised as legitimate application traffic
Typosquatting on package registries (e.g., publishing packages with names similar to popular libraries)
Dependency confusion attacks exploiting how package managers resolve internal vs public packages
Obfuscated code inserted to avoid detection during code review

defender.title: Detecting Malicious Code in Dependencies
defender.description: Static analysis tools can scan source code and compiled binaries for suspicious patterns like obfuscated code, unexpected network communications, or calls to sensitive system APIs. Package analysis tools like Socket.dev for npm specifically look for supply chain attack indicators such as install scripts that run arbitrary code, unexpected network access, or filesystem operations. Sandboxed execution of new software versions before deployment into production can reveal hidden behaviors like C2 communication. Comparing the vendor-provided binary against an independently compiled version (if source is available) can detect build pipeline compromises that insert code not present in the source repository.
tools_or_indicators: Static analysis scanning for suspicious patterns in dependencies
Socket.dev analyzing npm packages for supply chain attack indicators
Sandboxed execution of new versions before production deployment
Binary analysis comparing vendor builds against independent compilations
Runtime monitoring for unexpected network or filesystem behavior

victim.title: Malicious Code Embedded in Trusted Software
victim.description: A trusted piece of software that the organization uses daily now contains a hidden backdoor. The malicious code is buried within thousands or millions of lines of legitimate code, signed with a valid certificate, and distributed through official channels. It passed the vendor's quality assurance, code signing, and distribution processes because the attacker compromised those very processes. The organization has no practical way to detect the backdoor through its normal software intake procedures because everything about the update appears legitimate. This represents the fundamental challenge of supply chain security: you cannot be more secure than your weakest trusted supplier.
tools_or_indicators: Backdoored software appears identical to legitimate versions
Valid code signatures provide false sense of security
Malicious code hidden among millions of lines of legitimate code

attacker.title: Delivering Malware Through Legitimate Update Mechanisms
attacker.description: The compromised software update is distributed through the vendor's official update servers, package registry, or app store, the exact same channel that delivers legitimate updates. Organizations that have automatic updates enabled receive the backdoored version without any human intervention. The update passes all integrity checks because it is genuinely signed by the vendor. The attacker benefits from massive scale: a single compromised update can reach thousands or millions of systems simultaneously. This distribution mechanism is what makes supply chain attacks so efficient; the attacker compromises one point but gains access to the vendor's entire customer base.
tools_or_indicators: Official update servers distributing the compromised version
Automatic update mechanisms pulling the backdoored software
Package registries (npm, PyPI, Maven) serving the malicious package
Legitimate code signatures passing all integrity verification
CDN distribution amplifying the reach to all global users

defender.title: Controlling Software Deployment and Updates
defender.description: Organizations should never allow automatic updates from any vendor directly to production systems. A staged deployment model where updates first go to an isolated testing environment, then to a small pilot group, and only then to the broader organization provides time to detect anomalies before mass deployment. Network monitoring should baseline normal software update traffic patterns so that unusual behaviors in newly deployed versions (like unexpected outbound connections or DNS queries) trigger alerts. For critical software, maintaining the ability to quickly roll back to a previous known-good version is essential.
tools_or_indicators: Staged deployment model: test, pilot, then production
Network baselining to detect unusual behavior in new software versions
Ability to quickly roll back to previous known-good versions
Software whitelisting preventing unauthorized applications
Change management processes requiring approval for all software updates

victim.title: Receiving the Compromised Update
victim.description: The organization's automated update system downloads and installs the backdoored software version, or a developer runs 'npm install' and pulls the compromised package into their project. The update appears completely normal: it comes from the correct server, passes signature verification, and may even include legitimate bug fixes and features alongside the hidden backdoor. If automatic updates are enabled, the compromised software may be running on every relevant system in the organization within hours. The organization's own update infrastructure, designed to keep systems secure and current, has become the delivery mechanism for the attack.
tools_or_indicators: Automatic updates installing the compromised version across the organization
Package managers pulling the backdoored dependency
All standard integrity checks passing despite the embedded malware

attacker.title: Exploiting Access in Target Organizations
attacker.description: With the backdoor deployed across thousands of organizations, the attacker selectively activates it in their chosen targets. Not every infected organization is exploited; the attacker prioritizes high-value targets like government agencies, defense contractors, and major corporations. The backdoor provides initial access that the attacker then expands through standard post-exploitation techniques: credential harvesting, lateral movement, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration. Because the backdoor exists within trusted software that typically has elevated privileges and network access, the attacker starts from a much stronger position than a typical phishing-based compromise would provide.
tools_or_indicators: Selective activation of the backdoor in high-value target organizations
C2 communication established through the compromised software's network access
Credential harvesting and lateral movement from the privileged position of trusted software
Data exfiltration using the software's existing network permissions
Long-term persistent access through the trusted software's ongoing presence

defender.title: Detecting and Responding to Supply Chain Compromise
defender.description: Detecting a supply chain compromise requires monitoring for behavioral anomalies in trusted software: unexpected network connections, unusual process spawning, file system access outside the software's normal scope, and DNS queries to previously unseen domains. Threat intelligence sharing is critical because supply chain attacks affect many organizations simultaneously; participating in ISACs (Information Sharing and Analysis Centers) and monitoring vendor security advisories helps organizations learn about compromises discovered by others. When a supply chain compromise is confirmed, the response must include isolating all systems running the affected software, conducting a full investigation to determine if the backdoor was activated in your environment, and planning for the possibility that the attacker has already established independent persistence.
tools_or_indicators: Behavioral monitoring for anomalies in trusted software
Threat intelligence sharing through ISACs and industry groups
Vendor security advisory monitoring
Network traffic analysis for unexpected C2 communication
Full forensic investigation of all systems running affected software
Assuming breach and hunting for independent persistence mechanisms

victim.title: Compromised Through a Trusted Vendor
victim.description: The organization has been compromised not through any failure of their own security but through the trust they placed in a vendor. Their firewalls, endpoint protection, email filtering, and security training were all irrelevant because the attack came through an officially sanctioned software update. The backdoor may have been active for weeks or months before discovery, during which the attacker had access to the organization's most sensitive systems and data. Recovery is complex because the organization must not only remove the compromised software but also investigate and remediate any additional access the attacker established during the period of compromise. Supply chain attacks represent the most challenging threat in modern cybersecurity because they undermine the fundamental trust model that organizations depend on.
tools_or_indicators: Compromise bypassed all perimeter and endpoint security controls
Backdoor potentially active for weeks or months before discovery
Recovery requires removing compromised software AND all attacker persistence
Fundamental trust in vendor relationship has been violated
